articles.title: The Bottleneck Moved: AI Coding Agents Write 30% More Code, but Teams Ship the Same
articles.excerpt: Most teams that adopted AI coding agents expected one thing: ship faster. A new Harvard working paper on 718 companies suggests they got the opposite of the metric that matters. Code volume rose about…
articles.body: Most teams that adopted AI coding agents expected one thing: ship faster. A new Harvard working paper on 718 companies suggests they got the opposite of the metric that matters. Code volume rose about 30%, but delivered output barely moved — and time spent on code review jumped 49%. The bottleneck didn't disappear. It moved downstream. Why review became the choke point Three forces collide here. First, generation is cheap and reviewing is not. An agent can produce in seconds what a human needs twenty minutes to verify. Second, agent-written code is often plausible — it reads well, passes a glance, and hides subtle issues in the exact places reviewers skim. Third, review capacity is fixed. You can't autoscale the senior engineer who understands the domain.
articles.author: SkillStack

articles.title: Explaining Technical Concepts Is a Metaphor Problem, Not a Drawing Problem
articles.excerpt: I've spent years delivering technical projects, and I keep running into the same thing: when a concept fails to land, it's rarely because the diagram was bad. It's because the metaphor was wrong. Here…
articles.body: I've spent years delivering technical projects, and I keep running into the same thing: when a concept fails to land, it's rarely because the diagram was bad. It's because the metaphor was wrong. Here's a concrete case. Explaining caching, I'd draw the usual boxes: request comes in, check cache, hit returns early, miss goes downstream. Correct — and useless. Clients would nod, then ask: "so where exactly do we save?" Boxes and arrows describe what , not why . If the listener doesn't already understand the mechanism, the diagram doesn't help. A different approach: draw the object, not the flow Anatomy (7459 stars, MIT) takes the opposite route.

articles.title: Kafka and Flink Hit a Wall at the Model Serving Boundary
articles.excerpt: TL;DR — Kafka/Flink pipelines are built around record-at-a-time, backpressure-aware processing, while model servers get their throughput from batching requests together. The seam between the two is wh…
articles.body: TL;DR — Kafka/Flink pipelines are built around record-at-a-time, backpressure-aware processing, while model servers get their throughput from batching requests together. The seam between the two is where real-time AI pipelines quietly lose their latency guarantees. Fixing it means re-batching the stream right before the model boundary, not just scaling async capacity. Every real-time AI architecture diagram looks the same: Kafka topic, Flink job computing features, arrow pointing to a model server, latency number in the corner looking respectable. Nobody draws the part that actually breaks. The seam between the stream processor and the model server is not a plumbing detail.

articles.body: Most programming articles teach one concept well and then stop. Real engineering work rarely looks like that. Developers need end-to-end problem solving, the ability to take a messy requirement from a first idea to software that runs, gets maintained, and keeps working after the launch party ends. This article argues that modern programming content should be built around that full journey rather than around isolated syntax. Why Isolated Tutorials Fall Short A typical tutorial explains how a decorator works, how a hook manages state, or how a query joins two tables. Each explanation is accurate, and each one helps.

articles.title: Kubernetes readiness gates and rolling deploys without downtime
articles.excerpt: You ship a new version on a quiet Tuesday afternoon. kubectl rollout status reports success, every pod is Running and Ready, and the dashboards look fine. Then someone notices a small spike of 502s in…
articles.body: You ship a new version on a quiet Tuesday afternoon. kubectl rollout status reports success, every pod is Running and Ready, and the dashboards look fine. Then someone notices a small spike of 502s in the load balancer logs, lined up exactly with the deploy. Not enough to page anyone. Enough that a few hundred users got an error page for no reason. This happens on almost every cluster that has never been tuned for it. Kubernetes rolling updates are safe by default in the sense that they will not take your whole service down. They are not zero downtime by default. The gaps are at the edges of a pod's life: the moment a new pod starts taking traffic, and the moment an old one stops. I covered readiness and liveness probes themselves in an earlier article .

articles.title: The great Halley's Comet disappointment of 1986 — and the discoveries that changed astronomy forever
articles.excerpt: What disappointed skywatchers in 1986 became a scientific triumph, as an international fleet of spacecraft revealed the secrets of the world's most famous comet.
articles.body: This year, 2026, marks the 40th anniversary of the most recent appearance of Halley's Comet, the most famous comet in the solar system. Roughly every 76 years, Halley punctuates history like an exclamation mark in the night sky. As writer Guy Ottewell has said, it is the "wildest of the tame comets." It is a tame comet because it can be anticipated. It is wild because it is still fresh and bright; the brightest of all the recurring comets. It is the only one that periodically becomes conspicuous to the naked eye. Halley through history Before 1986, Halley had been seen and recorded on 29 occasions. In A.D. 66, observers described it as a sword in the skies above Jerusalem.

articles.body: Running my dream menagerie in Planet Zoo is always going to feel a little different than the entertainment-focused spectacles of Planet Coaster or fantastical dino parks of Jurassic World Evolution. All of these gorgeous beasts and birds are real species we share the planet with and, in some cases, have put on the endangered list. So I was glad to see that Frontier's sequel put an even deeper emphasis on conservation as a main goal this time around, even if certain pieces of that – like wildlife reserves – feel a bit less fleshed-out than they could be. When it comes to the daily tasks of building enclosures, hiring staff, and caring for animals, there isn't a ton that has changed since the original Planet Zoo .
